notes.b: Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist, proposed continental drift in 1912 and published it in his book The Origin of Continents and Oceans in 1915.
points: Wegener proposed that the continents were once joined in one supercontinent, Pangaea, surrounded by one ocean, Panthalassa, and have since drifted apart.
Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, separated by the Tethys Sea; these broke up further into today's continents.
Pangaea began to break up about 200 million years ago.
Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents, so the theory was rejected at first.
Jigsaw fit: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit together, and the fit is even better at the edge of the continental shelves.

Fossils: Mesosaurus, a small freshwater reptile, is found in both Brazil and southern Africa; Glossopteris, a fern-like plant, is found in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia. Neither could have crossed an ocean.
Rocks and mountains: the Appalachian Mountains of eastern North America match the Caledonian mountains of Ireland, Scotland and Norway in rock type, age and structure.
Past climates: glacial deposits and striations about 300 million years old occur in India, Africa, South America and Australia, places now warm or near the equator.
Coal seams in Antarctica formed from plant matter in warm swamps.
Detailed mapping of the ocean floor by echo-sounding (sonar) followed the Second World War.
The mapping revealed long mid-ocean ridges with a central rift valley, and deep ocean trenches.
The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is about 16,000 km long.

notes.b: Sea-floor spreading supplied the mechanism that continental drift lacked.
points: Arthur Holmes, a British geologist, suggested in the late 1920s that mantle convection could move continents.
Harry Hess, an American geologist, proposed sea-floor spreading in the early 1960s.
1. Magma rises at mid-ocean ridges.
2. It cools to form new oceanic crust made of basalt.
3. The new crust pushes older crust away on both sides of the ridge.
4. Old crust is destroyed again at ocean trenches.
Age of rocks: oceanic rocks are youngest at the ridge and get progressively older with distance from it, symmetrically on both sides.
Sediment: ocean-floor sediment is thin or absent at the ridge and thicker further away.

Palaeomagnetism: the earth's magnetic field reverses from time to time. Iron minerals in cooling basalt line up with the field at that moment, so the ocean floor holds stripes of normal and reversed magnetism that mirror each other on either side of the ridge.
Magnetic striping was explained by Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews in 1963.
Diagram: plan view of a ridge with symmetrical magnetic stripes and arrows showing movement away from the ridge.
A plate is a rigid slab of lithosphere that floats and moves on the asthenosphere. A plate can carry continental crust, oceanic crust or both.
The earth has seven major plates: Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic.
Smaller plates include Nazca, Cocos, Caribbean, Juan de Fuca, Philippine, Arabian and Scotia.
Some maps split the Indo-Australian plate into the Indian plate and the Australian plate; both versions are accepted. The Pacific plate is the largest.
Convection currents in the mantle drag the plates along.
Higher Level: ridge push is new, hot crust at the ridge sliding away from it under gravity; slab pull is the cold, dense subducting edge of a plate pulling the rest of the plate after it.
Plates move a few centimetres a year, so the map of continents and oceans changes over geological time. The Atlantic is widening by about 2.5 cm a year, roughly the rate a fingernail grows.

Plates meet in three ways: moving apart (constructive, or divergent), moving together (destructive, or convergent), and sliding past (passive, conservative, or transform). Each is described in the next subsection.
Plate movement drives endogenic forces, which are concentrated mostly along plate boundaries.
The continental drift and sea-floor spreading evidence above is why the plate tectonics model replaced the earlier theory.

notes.b: Ireland's position on the plate map determines its present geological activity.
points: Ireland lies on the Eurasian plate, near its western edge and far from any plate boundary.
The nearest plate boundary is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge to the west, which separates the Eurasian and North American plates.
As the Atlantic widens, Ireland moves slowly away from North America.
Ireland has no active volcanoes and only rare, minor earthquakes.

Before the Caledonian folding, Ireland was in two parts on opposite sides of the Iapetus Ocean: the north-west part on the North American (Laurentian) side and the south-east part on the European side.

The Iapetus Ocean closed as the plates converged, and the two parts of Ireland were joined along the Iapetus suture, which runs across Ireland roughly from the Shannon Estuary to Clogherhead, Co. Louth.
The collision caused the Caledonian folding, about 400 million years ago, which built mountains running north-east to south-west.
Caledonian mountains include the mountains of Donegal, Mayo and Connemara, and the Wicklow Mountains; the Leinster granite batholith was intruded during this period.
Ireland has drifted north over hundreds of millions of years.
Old Red Sandstone formed in hot, dry conditions after the Caledonian folding.
Carboniferous limestone formed about 350 million years ago, when Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow tropical sea.
The Armorican (Variscan) folding, about 300 million years ago, came from the collision of Africa, part of Gondwanaland, with Europe as Pangaea came together.
It built east-west mountains across the south of Ireland: Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdowns and the Caha Mountains, which form the Munster ridge-and-valley landscape.
Armorica is the old name for Brittany, where the same fold belt occurs.

notes.h: Opening of the Atlantic and Alpine folding
points: As North America and Greenland separated from Europe after Pangaea split, magma rose through cracks in north-east Ireland and formed the Antrim basalts about 60 million years ago.
Alpine folding is the most recent period of fold mountain building, producing the Alps and the Himalayas.
Alpine folding did not build Ireland's mountains; the two periods that did are Caledonian and Armorican.

keyTerms.definition: The supercontinent that Wegener proposed existed before the continents drifted apart.
The single ocean that surrounded Pangaea.
The process by which magma rises at mid-ocean ridges, cools to form new oceanic crust and pushes older crust away on both sides.
Evidence from iron minerals in cooling rock that records the direction of the earth's magnetic field at the time the rock formed.
A rigid slab of lithosphere that floats and moves on the asthenosphere.
The sliding of new, hot crust away from a mid-ocean ridge under gravity.
The pulling of the rest of a plate by its cold, dense subducting edge.
The line across Ireland along which the two parts of Ireland were joined when the Iapetus Ocean closed.
Fold mountain building caused by the closing of the Iapetus Ocean, producing north-east to south-west mountains in Ireland.
Fold mountain building caused by the collision of Africa with Europe, producing east-west mountains across the south of Ireland.

factCards.term: Plate tectonics theory: three scientists and their ideas
factCards.definition: Alfred Wegener, a German meteorologist: continental drift, 1912. Arthur Holmes, a British geologist: in the late 1920s, that mantle convection could move continents. Harry Hess, an American geologist: sea-floor spreading, early 1960s.

factCards.term: Continental drift: Wegener's book and how Pangaea broke up
factCards.definition: Wegener published The Origin of Continents and Oceans in 1915. Pangaea began to break up about 200 million years ago into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, separated by the Tethys Sea; these broke up into today's continents.

factCards.term: Continental drift evidence: jigsaw fit and fossils
factCards.definition: South America and Africa fit together, best at the edge of the continental shelves. Mesosaurus, a freshwater reptile, is found in Brazil and southern Africa; Glossopteris, a fern-like plant, in South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia.

factCards.term: Continental drift evidence: matching mountains and past climates
factCards.definition: The Appalachians of eastern North America match the Caledonian mountains of Ireland, Scotland and Norway in rock type, age and structure. Glacial deposits about 300 million years old occur in India, Africa, South America and Australia; coal in Antarctica.

factCards.term: Why continental drift was rejected at first, and what rescued it
factCards.definition: Wegener could not explain what force moved the continents. Sea-floor spreading later supplied the missing mechanism and turned continental drift into the theory of plate tectonics.

factCards.term: Mapping the ocean floor: what echo-sounding revealed
factCards.definition: Detailed sonar mapping after the Second World War revealed long mid-ocean ridges with a central rift valley, and deep ocean trenches. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is about 16,000 km long.

factCards.term: Sea-floor spreading: who proposed it, and what happens at ridges and trenches
factCards.definition: Harry Hess, an American geologist, early 1960s: magma rises at mid-ocean ridges and cools to form new basalt crust, which pushes older crust away on both sides; crust is destroyed again at ocean trenches.

factCards.term: Sea-floor spreading evidence: age of rocks and sediment
factCards.definition: Oceanic rocks are youngest at the ridge and get progressively older with distance from it, symmetrically on both sides. Ocean-floor sediment is thin or absent at the ridge and thicker further away.

factCards.term: Magnetic striping: how it proves sea-floor spreading
factCards.definition: The magnetic field reverses from time to time; iron minerals in cooling basalt line up with it, so the ocean floor holds stripes of normal and reversed magnetism mirrored either side of the ridge. Fred Vine and Drummond Matthews explained this in 1963.

factCards.term: Name the seven major lithospheric plates and four smaller ones
factCards.definition: Major: Pacific (the largest), North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian (or Indian and Australian) and Antarctic. Smaller: any four of Nazca, Cocos, Caribbean, Juan de Fuca, Philippine, Arabian and Scotia.

factCards.term: How plates move: three driving forces
factCards.definition: Convection currents in the mantle drag the plates; ridge push, as new, hot crust slides away from the ridge under gravity; slab pull, as the cold, dense subducting edge of a plate pulls the rest of the plate after it.

factCards.term: How fast plates move: the Atlantic figure
factCards.definition: Plates move a few centimetres a year; the Atlantic is widening by about 2.5 cm a year, roughly the rate a fingernail grows, so the map of continents and oceans changes over geological time.

factCards.term: Ireland's plate position today and its consequences
factCards.definition: Ireland is on the Eurasian plate, near its western edge and far from any boundary; the nearest is the Mid-Atlantic Ridge to the west, so Ireland moves slowly away from North America. It has no active volcanoes and only rare, minor earthquakes.

factCards.term: Iapetus Ocean: Ireland's two halves and where they joined
factCards.definition: About 500 million years ago north-west Ireland lay on the North American (Laurentian) side of the Iapetus Ocean and the south-east on the European side. As it closed they joined along the Iapetus suture, roughly Shannon Estuary to Clogherhead, Co. Louth.

factCards.term: Caledonian folding: date and named Irish mountains
factCards.definition: About 400 million years ago, as the Iapetus Ocean closed. It built north-east to south-west mountains: those of Donegal, Mayo and Connemara, and the Wicklow Mountains; the Leinster granite batholith was intruded in this period.

factCards.term: Armorican folding: date, cause and named Irish mountains
factCards.definition: About 300 million years ago, when Africa (part of Gondwanaland) collided with Europe as Pangaea came together. It built east–west ridges across the south: Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtee Mountains, the Knockmealdowns and the Caha Mountains.

factCards.term: Ireland's drift north: what two rock types record
factCards.definition: Old Red Sandstone formed in hot, dry conditions after the Caledonian folding; Carboniferous limestone formed about 350 million years ago, when Ireland lay near the equator under a warm, shallow tropical sea.

factCards.term: Antrim basalts: link to the opening of the Atlantic
factCards.definition: As North America and Greenland separated from Europe after Pangaea split, magma rose through cracks in north-east Ireland and formed the Antrim basalts about 60 million years ago.

factCards.term: Alpine folding: what it built, and why it is not Irish
factCards.definition: The most recent period of fold mountain building, producing the Alps (the African plate colliding with the Eurasian plate) and the Himalayas. It did not build Ireland's mountains; the two Irish periods are Caledonian and Armorican.

questions.prompt: Discuss the theory of plate tectonics.
questions.model: Continental drift: Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents were once joined in Pangaea, surrounded by Panthalassa, and drifted apart; his evidence was the jigsaw fit of South America and Africa, the fossils of Mesosaurus and Glossopteris, matching rocks and mountains such as the Appalachians and the Caledonian mountains, and past climates shown by glacial deposits and coal seams. Wegener could not explain the force that moved the continents. Sea-floor spreading: mapping by echo-sounding revealed mid-ocean ridges and trenches; Hess proposed that magma rises at ridges, forms new basaltic crust and pushes older crust away, destroyed at trenches. Evidence: rocks get older with distance from the ridge, sediment thickens away from the ridge, and palaeomagnetic stripes mirror each other on either side of the ridge. Plate tectonics: the lithosphere is broken into rigid plates that move on the asthenosphere; convection currents in the mantle drag them, and ridge push and slab pull are the Higher Level mechanisms. Plates meet at constructive, destructive and passive (transform) boundaries.

questions.prompt: Examine the position of Ireland in relation to plate boundaries now and in past geological periods.
questions.model: Now: Ireland lies on the Eurasian plate far from any plate boundary, with the Mid-Atlantic Ridge to the west, so it has no active volcanoes and only rare, minor earthquakes. Past: Ireland was in two parts on opposite sides of the Iapetus Ocean. When the Iapetus closed, the two parts were joined along the Iapetus suture and the Caledonian folding built north-east to south-west mountains such as Donegal, Mayo, Connemara and the Wicklow Mountains. Ireland drifted north; Old Red Sandstone formed in hot, dry conditions after the Caledonian folding, and Carboniferous limestone formed near the equator in a warm tropical sea. The Armorican folding, from the collision of Africa with Europe, built east-west mountains across the south, including Macgillycuddy's Reeks, the Galtees, the Knockmealdowns and the Caha Mountains. As Pangaea split and the Atlantic opened, magma formed the Antrim basalts about 60 million years ago.

questions.prompt: Name the plate Ireland lies on and explain briefly how plates move.
questions.model: Ireland lies on the Eurasian plate. Plates move because convection currents in the mantle drag them.
